learn.intro: A broad question like "is this a good review?" hides several judgments in one answer. Break it into small yes or no questions, let Jev answer each, and let code combine them with weights you choose. You can see why the score is what it is, and change it without asking Jev again.

compare.title: Jev, asked one broad question
points: One Noul for the whole judgment
You get a verdict, not the reasons behind it

compare.title: An LLM, asked the same broad question
points: Reads the review and answers true or false
Pays for every token it writes
You get a verdict, not the reasons behind it

compare.title: Jev + Code, five small questions
points: Jev answers five small Nouls per review
Code combines them with your weights
Change a weight and the score changes at once

predict.intro: On the Play step, Jev and an LLM each read the same 6 product reviews and answer one broad question about each: would this review help someone decide whether to buy? After that you see Jev answer five small questions per review instead. For now, guess about the broad question.

questions.prompt: Who answers the broad question for all 6 reviews first?
Who costs less for all 6 reviews?
Who judges more of the 6 reviews correctly?

tasks.title: Five small questions, combined in code

why: Small questions are easier to answer and easier to check. The code that combines them is plain arithmetic, so it never drifts and costs nothing.
The weights are yours: if tone matters more to you than detail, turn it up and the same Jev answers give a different score. The broad question has no such dial.
On this set the broad question was already accurate for every racer. The gain here is not accuracy, it is that you can see and tune the reasons.

questions.prompt: Why ask Jev five small questions per review and combine the answers in code, instead of one broad question?

options.text: You can see each reason and change its weight
It is always faster than one question
It makes Jev free to run

questions.explanation: Each small answer is a visible reason, and the weights are plain code you control. It is not always faster, and Jev still costs a little per question.

questions.prompt: You turn the weight of one small question to zero. What happens to the score?

options.text: Jev must be asked everything again

questions.explanation: The combining step is code. A zero weight just leaves that answer out, with no new call to Jev.
